Temporal Gradient Denoising is a technique that reduces noise in volume rendering by applying temporal reprojection and blending to gradient images rather than the final radiance image [S1, S2].

The claim states that Temporal Gradient Denoising reduces noise in volume rendering by applying temporal reprojection and blending to gradient images rather than the final radiance image. Both Source [S1] and Source [S2] explicitly confirm this. They describe the method as performing temporal denoising on gradient images (specifically gradients with respect to albedo) using reprojection and blending. Both sources also explicitly state that denoising the gradient is preferred over denoising the original (radiance) image because artifacts are not directly visible in the gradient. The specific parameters (w_a = 0.1, N = 11) and the mathematical formulation provided in the claim match the evidence in the sources.
supported

It solves the problem of high noise levels in Monte Carlo volume rendering, particularly in high-order scattering-dominant media, while avoiding the visible bias and artifacts that occur when denoising the original image directly [S1, S2].

The evidence in both Source [S1] and Source [S2] explicitly states that the proposed method involves denoising gradient images rather than the original radiance image. Both sources confirm that this approach avoids visible bias and artifacts that occur when denoising the original image directly. Furthermore, Source [S2] specifically highlights the context of 'high-order scattering-dominant media' (where light paths are long and noise is high) and presents the method as a solution to reduce noise in this context. Source [S1] also discusses participating media and shows results for scenes with high scattering. Therefore, the claim is fully supported by the provided text.

The first formula provided is the standard interpretation of the weighted sum described in [S1] and the intent of [S2].

The claim states that the first formula provided is the standard interpretation of the weighted sum described in [S1] and the intent of [S2]. However, the evidence shows a discrepancy in the formula for G_denoised(i) between the two sources. Source [S1] defines the formula as G_denoised(i) = [Σ w_a^k (1-w_a)^{-1} G_k(f_proj(i))] / [1 - (1-w_a)^N]. Source [S2] defines the formula as G_denoised(i) = [Σ w_a^k (1 - (1-w_a)^{-1} (1-w_a) G_k(f_proj^{-1}(i)) ) ]^{-1} (with some OCR artifacts, but clearly involving f_proj^{-1} and a different structure). Specifically, [S2] uses the reciprocal reprojection function f_proj^{-1} and has a different algebraic structure compared to [S1]. Therefore, the formula in [S1] is not the same as the intent/formula in [S2], making the claim that it represents the intent of [S2] unsupported by the evidence.
